99acbd1c7c0e7c2b: PETALING JAYA: Penganalisis berpendapat Bersatu tidak mampu terus berlengah dalam menentukan masa depannya bersama Perikatan Nasional (PN) kerana berisiko menjejaskan kedudukan politiknya dan sokongan di peringkat akar umbi.
Asrul Sani daripada Asia Group berkata, Bersatu mengambil masa terlalu lama untuk menerima hakikat PN tidak lagi menawarkan masa depan politik berdaya maju kepadanya.
Tegasnya, PAS telah memutuskan hubungan dengan Bersatu, manakala Wawasan secara efektif mengambil alih peranan sebagai rakan nasionalis Melayu pilihan parti Islam itu.

"Bersatu patut meninggalkan PN dan membina masa depan di luar gabungan itu. Terus kekal dalam PN hanya berisiko menyebabkan lebih ramai ahli keluar parti, melemahkan semangat akar umbi serta ketidakpastian berterusan berhubung agihan kerusi dan kerjasama pilihan raya, manakala PAS serta Wawasan mengambil alih ruang politiknya."
Beliau mengulas tindakan Jawatankuasa Bersatu Kangar, termasuk kepimpinan Pemuda dan Wanita serta "90 ketua cawangan" meninggalkan parti itu untuk menyertai Wawasan.
Ia menyusul sehari selepas Timbalan Ketua Bersatu Padang Besar, Ramzi Udi bersama 19 lagi pemimpin dan ahli parti meninggalkan parti itu kerana tidak berpuas hati dengan kepimpinannya.

Asrul berkata, semakin lama Presiden Bersatu, Muhyiddin Yassin mengekalkan parti itu terikat dengan PN, semakin jelas ia kelihatan tersekat dan gagal menyesuaikan diri dengan perubahan landskap politik.

Jelasnya, meninggalkan PN akan menyebabkan Bersatu kehilangan jenama gabungan itu serta akses kepada jentera akar umbi PAS yang ampuh, selain ia akan berdepan pertembungan pelbagai penjuru tanpa rakan kongsi jelas.

Tetapi, katanya, jika Bersatu memilih meninggalkan PN, parti itu berpeluang mendefinisikan semula identitinya, meneroka kerjasama baharu serta memfokuskan negeri dan kawasan lebih realistik untuk dimenangi.

"Jentera akar umbi mengambil masa bertahun-tahun untuk dibina dan tidak boleh diwujudkan secara tergesa-gesa menjelang pilihan raya. Risiko meninggalkan PN memang besar, tetapi risiko jangka panjang ialah tidak relevan dari segi politik."
Apa strategi Muhyiddin?
Asrul berkata, Muhyiddin mungkin mempunyai beberapa strategi tersembunyi yang berpotensi menggugat rancangan pilihan raya PAS, tetapi PN tidak patut menjadi tumpuan strategi Bersatu.
"Menggunakan kelebihan itu demi menyukarkan langkah PAS atau Wawasan hanya membuang masa dan sumber tanpa membina masa depan politik berdaya maju untuk partinya."

Jelasnya, Bersatu tidak boleh membina masa depannya dengan cuba menyaingi PAS atau Umno dalam hal ehwal Melayu kerana dua parti itu mempunyai akar lebih kukuh serta identiti lebih jelas, manakala Bersatu hanya mampu pergi sejauh itu dan mengehadkan daya tarikannya kepada kaum lain.

"Muhyiddin perlu mengemukakan visi meyakinkan untuk negara, termasuk ekonomi, tadbir urus dan masa depan Malaysia," katanya sambil menambah meninggalkan PN tanpa strategi lebih luas hanya akan mengubah kedudukan Bersatu tanpa menangani masalah asas berkaitan identiti dan hala tujunya.
Azmi Hassan daripada Akademi Nusantara berpendapat, Muhyiddin masih mempunyai urusan belum selesai, sebab itu Bersatu masih bersama PN.
Katanya, Muhyiddin mungkin cuba menunjukkan beliau masih berkuasa menentukan hala tuju Bersatu dan PN, walaupun berisiko merosakkan gabungan itu.

"Tindakan PAS setakat ini menunjukkan parti itu tidak lagi menganggap Bersatu sebagai sebahagian daripada PN," katanya sambil merujuk pengecualian Bersatu daripada perbincangan agihan kerusi antara PN dan Barisan Nasional bagi PRN Melaka.
Bersatu turut mendakwa PAS meminggirkan parti itu sebelum PRN Negeri Sembilan dengan tidak mempelawanya menyertai mesyuarat PN bagi rundingan kerusi.

Bersatu bertanding menggunakan logonya sendiri dan tewas di semua 22 kerusi ditandinginya dalam PRN Negeri Sembilan. PN pula memenangi tujuh daripada 36 kerusi, manakala BN menang 18 kerusi, dengan dua gabungan itu kemudiannya membentuk kerajaan negeri.
Azmi berkata, keputusan PRN Negeri Sembilan menunjukkan jenama PN masih mempunyai pengaruh besar dalam kalangan pengundi, yang menyukarkan Bersatu meninggalkan gabungan itu.
f4fefe1bad3c9014: KUALA LUMPUR: Allowing eatery operators to place tables and chairs on walkways is not a new policy, but an enhancement of guidelines established in 2017, said Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL).

Responding to queries about public safety concerns and regulatory enforcement, a DBKL spokesman said ongoing improvements to the framework aimed to ensure clearer, standardised implementation aligned with current needs.
"DBKL has not introduced any new policy allowing outdoor tables and chairs. The permit mechanism was already implemented previously.
"What is being done now is an improvement on existing guidelines to ensure execution is clearer, uniform and aligned with current requirements."
DBKL has moved to ease business operations for food premises operators by introducing improvements to streamline services and cut red tape.
It has given approval for operators to put tables and chairs on five-foot walkways with a RM30 monthly permit per table and chair.
The local authority also said outdoor seating approvals are not automatic and restricted to restaurants, eateries and cafes with suitable external space.
On public safety and pedestrian access, the spokesman gave an assurance that both issues remain the top priorities of DBKL when evaluating every application.
"Approvals are subject to conditions, including ensuring pedestrian walkways remain safe and unobstructed, the location is suitable and that it poses no risk to the public.
"Permit holders are responsible for maintaining safety in the approved areas throughout the permit period."
DBKL added that operators are forbidden from converting public parking bays into dining spaces.
"Parking bays are unauthorised areas for placing tables and chairs because their primary function must be maintained for public parking.
"Converting parking bays will reduce existing parking capacity in high-demand commercial areas, besides posing safety risks to patrons and disrupting traffic flow."
City Hall has conducted 319 operations, seizing 13,173 tables, chairs and other items that were placed illegally outside eateries from January to July this year.
This marked an increase from 286 operations last year, when 6,290 tables, chairs and other items were seized.

City Hall warned that action will be taken against non-compliant premises under By-law 46(1)(d) of the Street, Drainage and Building Act 1974 for placing tables and chairs without a permit or in violation of permit conditions.
381e673ad94f1b08: KUALA LUMPUR: Mooncakes, lanterns and family reunions may be the most familiar symbols of the Mid-Autumn Festival, but its roots lie in something more basic - the harvest.
Traditionally, the festival marked a time to give thanks after months of labour in the fields, when communities could pause and celebrate abundance before the next cycle began.
That older idea has been given a distinctly Malaysian interpretation in a seasonal art installation in Kuala Lumpur’s Chinatown, where rice takes centre stage.
Visitors walking through the Kwai Chai Hong heritage alley will encounter rice sack-inspired lanterns, padi stalks, and harvest imagery intended to evoke the journey from field to table.
The choice of rice is deliberate. Beyond being a staple food, it carries memories, habits and lessons familiar across Malaysian households.

Co-organiser Zeen Chang said the installation was partly inspired by the reminders many children grow up hearing at the dining table: do not waste food, remember the effort behind it, and be grateful for what you have.
She pointed to the Chinese saying “li li jie xin ku”, which conveys the hard work behind every grain, and the Malay expression “kalau tak habis makan, nanti nasi menangis".
Though different in language and origin, both encourage children to value food and recognise the labour behind it.
“Every grain of rice begins as a seed which, in turn, depends on fertile soil, favourable weather and countless hands before eventually reaching the table,” Chang told Bernama.
“That relationship between effort and abundance resonates across Malaysia’s cultures.”
The installation’s main pavilion draws inspiration from traditional rice mills and padi fields, using lanterns, rice sacks and rural motifs to bring that landscape into the city.
For visitors, the effect is less about faithfully recreating agricultural life than about making something ordinary feel visible again.

Chang said the story of rice is also one of interdependence. The rice eaten at one family’s table may have been planted, harvested, milled, transported and sold by people from entirely different communities.
That makes it an unexpectedly useful symbol for a festival often associated primarily with Chinese tradition.
Rice appears almost everywhere in Malaysian life - in homes, kopitiams, roadside stalls and restaurants, crossing ethnic and social boundaries with little fanfare.
“And perhaps it is precisely because it is so ordinary that its value can so easily be overlooked,” Chang said.
Another familiar object appears among the displays: the traditional rooster bowl, with its colourful bird motif and white ceramic body.
For many Malaysian Chinese families, the bowl is instantly recognisable from childhood kitchens, coffee shops and everyday meals, making it another object that connects memory with food.
The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on Sept 25 this year, and its contemporary celebrations may look very different from the farming communities that shaped its earliest traditions.
Yet the idea of harvest remains easy to understand, particularly in a country where food is such a central part of daily life.
It is a reminder that abundance rarely arrives on its own: behind a bowl of rice are weather, soil, labour, transport, and countless small acts and blessings that usually go unnoticed.
15606da004b8bca6: PETALING JAYA: Bersatu cannot afford to continue dragging its feet over its future in Perikatan Nasional without risking further damage to its political standing and support among the grassroots, an analyst says.
Bersatu is taking too long to accept that PN no longer offers the party a viable political future, said Asrul Sani of the Asia Group.
PAS has cut ties with the party, and Wawasan has effectively assumed the role of the Islamic party’s preferred Malay nationalist partner.

“Bersatu should leave PN and build a future beyond the coalition," Asrul said. "Staying risks further defections, weaker grassroots morale and continued uncertainty over seats and electoral cooperation, while PAS and Wawasan steadily absorb its political space."
He was commenting on the defection of the Kangar Bersatu division committee, along with leaders of its youth and women’s wings and “90 branch chiefs” who left the party to join Wawasan.

The latest defections come a day after Padang Besar Bersatu deputy chief Ramzi Udi and 19 other party leaders and members announced their departure from the party, citing dissatisfaction with its leadership.
Asrul said the longer that Bersatu president Muhyiddin Yassin keeps the party tied to PN, the more the party appears stuck and unable to respond to a political landscape that has already moved on.
On the one hand, leaving would cost Bersatu the PN brand and access to PAS’s formidable grassroots machinery, exposing it to multi-cornered contests without an obvious partner.
On the other hand, leaving PN would allow Bersatu to define its own identity, explore new partnerships and concentrate on states and constituencies where it has a realistic chance of winning.

“Grassroots machinery takes years to develop and cannot be recreated just before an election. The risks of leaving are considerable, but the longer-term risk of remaining is political irrelevance,” he warned.
What is Muhyiddin’s game?
Asrul said that Muhyiddin could still have some cards up his sleeve that could disrupt PAS’s electoral plans, but PN should no longer be central to Bersatu’s strategy.
“Using those cards merely to frustrate PAS or Wawasan would consume valuable time and resources without creating a viable future for the party,” he said.

Asrul also said Bersatu cannot build its future simply by trying to out-do PAS or Umno on Malay affairs: both its rivals have deeper roots and clearer identities, and Bersatu could go only so far and further limit its appeal beyond Malay voters.

“Muhyiddin needs to offer a credible vision for the country, including on the economy, governance and Malaysia’s future,” he said, adding that leaving PN without a broader strategy would only alter Bersatu’s position without addressing its deeper issues of identity and purpose.
Azmi Hassan of Akademi Nusantara said Muhyiddin still has a score to settle, which is why Bersatu has not made a move to leave PN.
He suggested that Muhyiddin may be trying to show he still calls the shots in Bersatu and PN, even at the risk of wrecking the coalition.
“PAS’s actions so far suggest it no longer sees Bersatu as part of PN,” he said, pointing to Bersatu’s exclusion from PN-Barisan Nasional talks on seat negotiations for the Melaka state election.
Bersatu had also claimed that PAS had sidelined the party prior to the Negeri Sembilan state election by not inviting the party to attend PN meetings on seat negotiations.

Bersatu contested the Negeri Sembilan polls under its logo and lost all its 22 contests. PN won seven of the total 36 seats, while BN secured 18, with the two coalitions subsequently forming the state government.
Azmi said the Negeri Sembilan polls showed that the PN brand still carries considerable weight among voters. This would make it difficult for Bersatu to simply walk away from the coalition.
3a61b25dcf6a49ea: NEW DELHI: Malaysia can take on high-value engineering work now being done in India if it develops the right skills, says a senior executive of French engineering group Segula Technologies.

Arun Rajendran, the Segula Technologies India and Southeast Asia CEO and managing director, said Malaysia already had strong car, aerospace, electronics, and semiconductor industries, along with good roads, ports and air links.
“Malaysia is seen more as a manufacturing hub,” he told FMT after meeting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on the sidelines of the BRICS leadership summit on Saturday.
Arun said much of the more specialised design and engineering work was still being carried out in countries such as India, but Malaysia could take on more of this work by training local engineers.
Segula plans to set up a global engineering centre in Malaysia by the end of 2026, according to the Prime Minister’s Office.
The centre will hire Malaysians and use Segula’s expertise in artificial intelligence to support the car, aerospace, energy, and manufacturing industries.
Arun said Segula’s global customers in the car and aerospace industries were already asking whether more work could be carried out in Malaysia instead of being sent back to India.
“We need people to deliver from Malaysia. That’s the need of the hour for all my customers," he said.
He said experienced engineers could initially be brought in from India to train Malaysian teams for about three to four months before local staff take over more of the work.
Arun said Malaysia was also becoming more attractive as skilled engineers in India became increasingly costly and harder to retain.
“India has also become very expensive. It’s not cheap anymore,” he said, adding that it was becoming more difficult to retain talent.
Segula is also in talks with HICOM Engineering on a possible partnership in Malaysia.
He said Malaysia’s other strengths included reliable power and water supply and the presence of many major international manufacturers.
3f07742f2acbb0bd: KUALA LUMPUR: The following is the royal address by the Sultan of Perak, Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah, titled "Building Resilience: The Intersection Between Capital, Climate and Innovation". It was delivered at the 17th SC-OCIS Roundtable, held at the Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies in the United Kingdom.
1. Whenever I walk beneath this building's dome, I am reminded that this Centre did not attain its grandeur easily or immediately.

The Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies, which celebrated its 40th anniversary last year, began, as many of you know, in a wooden hut on St Cross Road, funded by a donation that today would not cover the cost of a black cab from the airport. Yet from these humble beginnings back in 1985, a trust was slowly built between scholars from West to East, from Rabat to Mecca to Kuala Lumpur, and a bridge of understanding developed between the intellectual traditions of Oxford and the Muslim world.

2. The beautiful structure around us stands as testament to that vision - a physical tribute to the joining of these two great traditions. A minaret, among the dreaming spires of Oxford, rising beside a quadrangle. Stone drawn from the English villages of Ketton and Clipsham, alongside Malaysian timber for the great auditorium. Every quadrangle here carries a name, and every name carries a debt of gratitude - the King Fahd Quad, the Oman Hall, the Istanbul Courtyard. This is not decoration. It is a physical shukr - a gratitude rendered in stone by many hands and many nations, in acknowledgment of the gift of knowledge that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has placed within reach of anyone bold enough to seek it.

3. Indeed, I could hardly imagine a more apt setting for the conversation we are here to have today. We have gathered to talk about resilience - how we build it, and how we maintain it - and this building is resilience embodied, raised up from something small and humble: a vision achieved through hard work and persistence. What's more, this building is, as I have mentioned already, a space for bringing together traditions that have not always been in conversation. That is what today is all about.

4. This year's Roundtable is convened around a theme of real consequence for our shared future, the building of resilience at the meeting point of capital, climate, and innovation. These three words are often spoken separately, as though they belong to different conversations held in different rooms. The premise of this Roundtable - and I believe it to be the correct one is that they belong together, and that our future depends upon our ability to unite these three priorities in pursuit of a shared goal.

5. Our world today is replete with dire warnings of the consequences of treating capital and the climate as unrelated concerns. The danger was foretold in an immensely thoughtful work by the late Dr Umer Chapra (d. 2026), titled The Islamic Vision of Development in the Light of Maqasid al-Shariah, published nearly two decades ago.

6. Chapra's argument, distilled, is this. Imam al-Ghazali (d. 1111), the great scholar of the Islamic Golden Age, identified five objectives that the Shariah exists to safeguard. These maqasid are faith, the human self, intellect, posterity, and wealth. Chapra insisted that wealth was never meant to stand alone. It is, in his words, "a trust from God" an amanah. He warned that a civilisation which pursues economic growth while neglecting the other four objectives may enjoy "relatively higher rates of growth" in the short term, but will pay for it in the long run, through inequity, family breakdown, and social unrest.

7. Chapra was writing about human development. He was not, primarily, writing about the state of the planet. And yet his framework naturally extends to it. He reminds us that the environment - "including animals, birds and insects" - is itself a trust, and must be protected, "so that no harm is done to the present or the future generations." Posterity, nasl, was one of his five pillars precisely because no generation is entitled to consume the inheritance of the next.

8. These observations acquire new significance when considered alongside recent events. Here in Oxford, and across Southern and Central Europe this summer, heatwaves have broken temperature records, governments have issued warnings to the elderly to stay indoors, and rivers have run low enough to strand barges. Almost three quarters of the United Kingdom a country, if you'll permit me, notorious for its rain - found itself in drought. And, looking beyond Europe, extreme weather events have claimed far too many lives, with the tragic floods in Nepal coming as the most recent and most devastating episode in a pattern of climate disasters. The environment, that sacred trust, has not been protected; and now Chapra's warning has moved from foresight into lived reality.

9. This escalating emergency is, without question, a consequence of human greed and thoughtlessness. For too long, humanity's purpose, on a global scale, has been growth for growth's sake. Shareholder profits, stock market performance, and GDP: these are what we measure, what we report on, how we judge success and progress. The Quran reminds us that "corruption has flourished on land and sea as a result of people's actions." We were placed upon this earth as its custodians, not its plunderers, and the account now falling due is one that our own conduct has written.

10. Now, I'm not here to pretend that growth isn't important. For a country such as Malaysia, on the path to high-income status, growth is hugely important, for the increased opportunities and broader horizons it brings to our people. But growth as an end in itself - growth driven by greed - this is a problem. Growth alone cannot be our purpose, our driving force as a human race.

11. Instead, we urgently need to bring growth into conversation with the climate emergency. The historic destruction of the environment in pursuit of wealth: that is what has landed us in this crisis. And capital, investment, must now get us out of it. The transition to a resilient and sustainable future cannot be financed by public treasuries alone. The sums required are vast, beyond the reach of any government acting by itself. Private capital, patiently and wisely deployed, must carry a substantial part of this burden. Yet capital, left entirely to its own instincts, tends toward the immediate and the certain. The task before the financial community is therefore to extend its horizons, to learn to price risks that unfold across decades rather than quarters, and to recognize that the returns which matter most in the end are those that endure.

12. This is where, I believe, the principles of Islamic finance can lead the way. A tradition that binds finance to the real economy, insists that capital serve productive and beneficial ends, shares risk rather than shifting it onto others, and forbids the reckless and the harmful this is most well suited to the demands of sustainable investment. We need sukuk structures, waqf-based mechanisms, and green and blue financing instruments that position impact ahead of commercial convenience. We need the courage to challenge attitudes and priorities, rather than fitting our solutions to the status quo: a financial industry that innovates boldly, and prices climate risk honestly modelled on Islamic finance. Indeed, what much of the world has lately begun to call responsible finance, our own tradition has long regarded simply as finance conducted properly.

13. In the context of our conversation today, a key role of responsible investment is, of course, to fund innovation - the third of our three forces. Human ingenuity has repeatedly confounded those who declared a problem to be unsolvable. The technologies of clean energy, efficient agriculture, water management and resilient construction are advancing at a pace that would have seemed improbable only a generation ago. In 2025, wind, solar and other renewables overtook coal as the world's leading source of electricity. For me, this is a sign of progress; and a cause for optimism.

14. Indeed, I firmly believe that research, discovery, and invention have the potential to navigate us through the climate crisis. But intent and motivation matter. According to our tradition, good innovation, bid'ah hasanah, is a tool, and a tool takes its worth from the hand that wields it and the purpose to which it is turned. Consider the story of DDT (Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane) - hailed in the mid-twentieth century as the miracle solution to insect-borne disease and crop loss, deployed at extraordinary scale until we discovered it was silently destroying the very ecosystems that sustained the crops it was meant to protect. Take also the more recent temptation of geoengineering - proposals to dim the sun itself with sulphate particles, to buy time, rather than to change course. Each of these innovations is technically ingenious. They also share the same flaw: they treat the symptoms of a mistreated planet, while leaving the disease of unrestrained appetite and growth for growth's sake entirely undisturbed.

15. Instead, what we need is targeted innovation, which is guided by and geared towards behavioural change, as well as technical fixes. Innovation must be underpinned, moreover, by thorough knowledge, hailed in our tradition as a sacred gift as the Quran says, "And He taught Adam the names of all things". When innovation is driven by the right purpose, and founded upon deep understanding, we see real change for the better. Scientific proof that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were responsible for the hole in the ozone layer led to global policy change, and as a result, the hole is shrinking. In 2025, the Antarctic ozone hole was the smallest and shortest-lived it had been in five years, confirming for scientists that policies aimed at phasing out ozone-depleting chemicals are having a real and positive impact.

16. Another, similar example is the reduction in acid rain across Europe and North America, which began towards the end of the twentieth century. Once scientists were able to prove that the acidity was caused by emissions of gases like sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, a combination of policy change and technical innovation helped reduce the emissions, which in turn helped reduce acid rainfall. As a result, the affected ecosystems for instance, freshwater lakes are beginning to recover, though acid rain of course remains a pressing issue across much of Asia.

17. From this last example, in particular, I believe there is much we can learn. Firstly, it is a sobering truth that scientific research into the causes of acid rain was initially curbed, and almost prevented altogether, by business interests that viewed the potential impact on their operations as a threat to profits. Influential voices with ulterior motives, protecting their own financial interests over the interests of the natural world: this remains a risk today. I say once again that we must not, we cannot, allow the pursuit of profit to get in the way of the protection of the planet - not least because, in the end, it is a false distinction. Only in the very short term can profit and the planet be considered opposing goals or values. If we fail to reverse the harm we have done to our planet, we will be worse off in all senses of the phrase. The near miss in the case of acid rain research, therefore, stands as a cautionary tale: a reminder to pursue what we know is right for the planet, even in the face of obstruction.

18. The second lesson I would draw from the successful reduction of acid rain is that, sometimes, the true innovation is for us, as humans, to do less. The temptation, in a crisis, is to throw more and more elaborate solutions into the mix - and these can have a valuable impact. But with acid rain, as with the hole in the ozone layer, what we really needed to do, above all else, was reduce our carbon footprint, put less into the environment, not more. With emissions lowered, the lakes whose ecosystems were wiped out by acid rain are gradually recovering on their own. Indeed, our planet's own resilience is nothing short of miraculous.

19. The process of climate recovery will take time. The impact of humanity's mistreatment of the planet did not reveal itself straight away, and the impact of our attempts to undo this damage will take even longer to materialise. We must be patient. We must respect the planet's own healing process. The positive changes we make today could take decades to manifest: and far from being a reason to delay those changes, this is, absolutely, the best reason we have to act now.

20. The Quran describes how, when people are tested - for instance, by a storm at sea - they turn to God with a sincerity that seems unshakeable. We saw this, I think, during the pandemic a brief, global moment of humility, of reflection, of neighbourliness. And we have watched it evaporate just as quickly. A test that is passed and then forgotten has taught us nothing. The measure of a community's faith is not what it does in the storm, but what it does once it reaches the shore.

21. When it comes to the climate emergency, we are, absolutely, in the middle of the storm. And I think there is global - though not unanimous - recognition that we need to act decisively, and act fast. But if we make it to the shore this time, it will not do to simply slip back into old habits, old motivations, and forget this lesson. We need to embed a change of purpose, attitude and behaviour for good. We need to unite the forces of capital and innovation in service of the climate, for a lasting impact and a truly resilient future.

22. Before closing, I want to add a word on justice, for it cannot be absent from this conversation. Those who have contributed least to the warming of our planet are very often those who suffer its consequences most acutely. The nations of the developing world, many of them young, populous, and rich in promise, did not create the greater part of this crisis, yet they stand the most exposed to it. True resilience cannot be built for some while it is denied to others. The capital and the innovation of which we speak must reach those who need them most, and not only those with the means to bear the financial cost.

23. To the young, in particular, I would say this. You will inherit the consequences of the choices made in rooms such as this one, and you are right to hold my generation to account for them. But I urge you to meet this inheritance not with despair, which only paralyses, but with resolve, which builds. Our Prophet sallallahu 'alayhi wassalam taught that even if the Final Hour itself were upon you, and you held a seedling in your hand, you should plant it even then. There is scarcely a wiser counsel from the Prophet for our age. We act, we build, and we plant, because the act itself is right, whatever the outcome may prove to be.

24. My hope for this Roundtable is therefore a practical one. That we leave it resolved to bring the capital we command, the innovation we pursue, and the responsibility we bear into a single and coherent effort. Let us build with the coming generations in mind, and not merely with an eye to the returns of the coming year. And let us remember that the Mother Earth we enjoy is a trust, to be handed on to those who follow us in no worse a condition than we ourselves received it.
25. May Allah grant us wisdom in the stewardship that has been entrusted to us, and make of our efforts a benefit that continues long after we are gone, amin!

1335278716a315f4: KUALA LUMPUR: A coalition of residents' associations is gravely disappointed with the government and Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) over the decision to allow restaurant operators to place tables and chairs on public walkways.

Save Kuala Lumpur (SKL) chairman Datuk M. Ali expressed deep frustration over the lack of public consultation and questioned why authorities are prioritising business operators over the safety and interests of residents.
"Where is the engagement with the people? Where is the minister's engagement with the people on this matter? Why are they so secretive about it?
"They implement and announce it... and let the people suffer. Where is the Madani spirit?" he told the New Sunday Times.
Ali was responding to DBKL's recent move to ease business operations for food premises operators by introducing improvements to streamline services and cut red tape across the federal capital.

This followed recent engagements between Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh, Kuala Lumpur Mayor Datuk Seri Fadlun Mak Ujud, the Selangor and Kuala Lumpur Chinese Coffee Shop and Tea Shop Owners' Association, and the Malaysia Muslim Restaurant Operators Association.
As part of the initiative, DBKL has given approval for restaurant operators to set up tables and chairs on five-foot walkways with a RM30 monthly permit per table and chair.
Ali said placing obstacles along pedestrian paths will pose a severe safety hazard to the public.
"They are putting people's lives at great risk. If the place is obstructed, what do I do? I can't wait for them to clear their crowds, so I have to step onto the road.
"When I step onto the road, I am exposed (to vehicles). What safety is City Hall providing us?"
He added that the decision directly contradicted DBKL's long-term urban planning framework, namely the Kuala Lumpur Local Plan 2040.

"This is in contravention of their own city plan. If in the 2040 plan you have identified specific pedestrian passageways, seamlessness and hindrance-free passageways, then why are you making backdoor provisions to create obstacles for pedestrians?"
Ali also blamed the government for allowing the initiative to move forward without grassroots feedback.
"I hold her (Yeoh) responsible. She should have struck it down and said, 'No, this is a no-go unless the people have expressed their interest or have no objection.'"
He said that the coalition would write officially to Yeoh and Fadlun, demanding an explanation on how the decision was reached.
Ali also called on all residents of Kuala Lumpur to raise their objections against the move.

"The people should object, protest and express concern. Go to the ADU@KL website and keep sending objections that this is not a fair deal. The interest and space of the people must be given due recognition," he said.
The New Sunday Times has reached out to Yeoh and Fadlun over the matter.
4bfa93df4a8de183: LOS ANGELES: OpenAI will not go public in 2026, CEO Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence.
"I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don't feel pressure on that," Altman told Fortune.

Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race ‌in the not-too-distant future.

The warnings follow cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology's risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action.

The New York Times in June reported that San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year. At the time, shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company's valuation to US$1.8 trillion.

When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said, "I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together."
Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development.
"We must slow the ‌pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote in an essay shared on social media.
Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment.

"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," Altman wrote in a response to Amodei's post on the X platform. "This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."

Safety concerns have not slowed down Anthropic's own IPO plans so far. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.
524edded530210a7: NEW DELHI: Chinese President Xi Jinping joined the leaders of Russia, Iran, India and other BRICS nations in New Delhi on Saturday, seeking common ground on the Middle East war as deep divisions test the 11-member bloc.
Xi told the summit that the Middle East war "does not serve the common interests of the international community", according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.

However, Indian diplomatic sources said leaders were working towards a joint position on some issues as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

"We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders.
Modi, opening the two-day summit, called for a system "where every country has a voice, every member has a stake, and humanity's development is at the centre of every effort."
He told leaders that BRICS nations "represent 50 perc ent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP, and more than 25 per cent of global trade."
The Middle East conflict was high on the agenda.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

Iran's Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a "regional policeman", with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.

Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also at the summit in New Delhi, as is Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan is expected to join later on Saturday.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
- 'HANDLING DIFFERENCES' -
But the summit's other major focus is China.
Xi's visit is also being closely watched because it is his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses, and greeted with a handshake by Modi at the summit venue.
His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said ahead of his visit that it was "ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences."
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500km high-altitude border with Tibet.
Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Modi later on Saturday, according to New Delhi's foreign ministry.
"They are looking for 'early and substantial harvest' when it comes to the border issue," said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
"You cannot have a build-up of your forces on the border... but at the same time say 'we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships'."
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday – exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 – waving placards against Xi's visit.--AFP

4989f9b2294c4322: KUALA LUMPUR: The Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution needs stronger political commitment, faster regional responses and greater accountability if the region is to break the cycle of recurring haze, experts said.

International Islamic University Malaysia political science lecturer Associate Professor Dr Tunku Mohar Tunku Mokhtar said the agreement's main weakness was its reliance on national measures, which could prove ineffective when pollution involved government or government-linked entities.
He said other mechanisms, including joint emergency responses and regional coordination, had also yet to produce results.
Previously, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the Asean mechanism on transboundary haze had room for improvement, as smoke from forest fires in Indonesia continued to affect Malaysia.
He said Asean ministers should review the mechanism given the impact of transboundary haze on public health.
Tunku Mohar said Asean's consensus-based decision-making could make reforms difficult.
"In the end, member states will end up with rhetoric of unity."
He also pointed to a lack of political will among member states, which had contributed to perceptions that governments could be complicit in allowing the problem to persist.
Asean's principle of non-interference was another hurdle, he said, although addressing a cross-border environmental problem should not be viewed as an infringement of national sovereignty.
"In some common issues such as transboundary haze, a call for a regional solution should not be understood as an attack on another state's sovereignty."
He said Asean needed to develop a stronger regional understanding that a clean environment was a basic human right and that addressing haze was a shared responsibility.
"If the cause of haze is natural, then affected members must allow other Asean members to assist in solving it.
"If it is caused by human activities, they should be stopped and punished."
Universiti Teknologi Mara senior political science lecturer Shahidah Abdul Razak said Asean should place greater emphasis on early intervention.

She said member states should respond more quickly when hotspots were detected, with faster information-sharing, clearer identification of fire sources and closer coordination between relevant agencies.
She said the recurring problem was driven by a combination of economic interests, land-clearing practices, enforcement challenges and weather conditions.
"Burning is still one of the cheaper ways to clear land, and during prolonged dry weather, fires can spread very quickly, especially on peatland.
"We have become better at detecting hotspots, but detecting a fire and preventing it from happening are two different things.
"When smoke crosses borders and affects people in neighbouring countries, it is no longer a domestic issue."

Shahidah said Asean needed to ensure that information gathered through its regional mechanisms translated into concrete action, including identifying those responsible for fires and establishing greater transparency around land ownership and control.
"At the end of the day, progress should not only be measured by how many meetings Asean holds, but whether we see fewer fires and haze episodes," she said.
