b8635022489761fd: GEORGE TOWN, Sept 13 — Before he was brining chicken and making coconut milk-laced romesco at Gilda Restaurant, Ahmad Soffian Salim was washing plates in restaurants more than 14 years ago.
It was almost an accidental career change for the mechanical engineering major who had initially worked in the engineering department at Malaysia Airlines planning aircraft maintenance and servicing.
Ahmad relocated to Melbourne, Australia with his wife, Aim Aris, back in 2012 when the latter was pursuing her postgraduate studies there.
Living in an area that was far from the airport, Ahmad sought out jobs near their home and ended up as a kitchen assistant washing dishes and pots in a restaurant.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Chef Ahmad working in the open kitchen.
”We lived in an area where one of the best cafes in Melbourne was just behind our house,” Aim said.
She said 2012 was the peak of cafe culture in the area and it was their first time experiencing the Australian hospitality industry where in some cafes, the chef designs the menu to pair with coffee.
”It was really interesting and that was the first spark for Ahmad to want to try immersing himself in this industry,” she said.
One of the easiest ways to get in was to work his way up so that was how Ahmad started working as a kitchen assistant.
”I love food but what really made me want to be a chef was the high quality local produce there,” Ahmad said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Gilda Lunch Spread is meant for sharing.
He said the locally sourced produce was of such good quality that the chefs did not really need to do much except to elevate it and let its natural flavours come through.

The couple had only expected to stay in Melbourne for about two years but it somehow stretched into eight as Ahmad worked his way up from a kitchen assistant to line cook to becoming the head chef of an Australian restaurant in five years.
“I worked in different cafes and restaurants and trained in modern Australian cuisine as my interest in cooking grew,” he said.
He had briefly considered applying to study in a culinary school but the fees were high while chefs in the restaurants he worked in encouraged him to learn on the job instead.
So, he took jobs in different kitchens to build his experience, going from working a morning shift in one restaurant and heading to another restaurant for dinner service.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Clockwise from left: Grilled sea bass, grilled chicken and roasted mushroom baguette.
“I was fully occupied working from morning until night time for five days kind of thing, I often worked two jobs during that time because I wanted to learn,” he said.
His appetite for learning was fuelled by what he found around him in Melbourne: cafes, restaurants, coffee and ingredients that opened up new possibilities.

After working his way up to become head chef and with Aim nearing the end of her PhD in late 2019, they decided to take one year off to travel and set up pop-up kitchens and collaborations in Jakarta, Hong Kong, Japan and Thailand.
However, the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted their plans.
The couple was in Penang to conduct research and work on a cookbook project in 2020.
“We managed to do our pop-up for three days—a kitchen takeover—at Norm Micro Roastery. And then the government announced a lockdown,” Ahmad said.
Interstate and international travel were prohibited and their plans to continue to Europe were put on hold.
It was then that they were asked to help plan a restaurant menu as a restaurant consultant.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Chef Ahmad and wife Aim manage the restaurant which is co-founded with three other investors.
“At that point, I had only ever been a chef, I didn’t know much about restaurant consultancy so we told the restaurant, we will try,” he recalled.
What was initially meant to be a month of assistance became nine months as they developed the menu, helped run the kitchen and trained the team.
For Ahmad, it was also his first experience working as a chef in Malaysia.
Aim said they decided to make the most of their circumstances since they were both stranded in Penang during the lockdown.
From the one consultancy project, it led to more projects including a one-year residency at a restaurant in Chinatown in Kuala Lumpur in 2023.
The residency gave Ahmad something he had missed while setting up kitchens for others: a kitchen where he could cook his own food with his own team.
They later helped with the menu planning, training and opening of Peninsula House in Penang in July 2024, before handing over to its team.
The birth of Gilda
After years of moving between projects, they started toying with the idea of opening their own restaurant.
”Since we are both from KL, our initial plan was to set up a place there,” Aim said.
Penang, however, had another connection waiting for them — a friendship formed through a small pop-up during the pandemic.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Gilda offers contemporary dining from brunch to dinner.
Among the guests was art collector and founder of Blank Canvas, Leong KY, who was also stranded in Penang at the time.
He subsequently invited the couple to cook for private dinners and gallery events in Penang.
“I would say he is our ‘lockdown friend’,” Ahmad said.
When Leong found a new space for Blank Canvas in Soo Hong Lane, it was larger than he needed.
He reached out to Ahmad and suggested they use the extra space beside the gallery as a restaurant.
They initially offered to consult instead but Leong wanted them to run and manage the place.
The idea gradually took hold. Their Penang project progressed while their Kuala Lumpur plans were delayed, prompting them to focus on Gilda.
The restaurant opened on October 25 last year, with five founders: Ahmad, Aim, Leong, Alfred Cheong and property owner Dickson Lim.
Ahmad and Aim oversee operations, while the space also doubles as a showcase of artworks from Leong’s personal collection.
”I chose the name Gilda because I wanted something short, easy to read and with the character of a female name, as I noticed Melbourne restaurants tend to use female names,” she said.

She said the word is old English for golden and gold is a good thing to associate with the restaurant as in terms of food, it also refers to golden crust, the crispness of cooking, the golden standard or food that is really nice.
At Gilda, Ahmad’s food reflects the kitchens he learnt in, without restricting him to a single cuisine.
His foundation is modern Australian cooking, which he sees as shaped by the food, traditions and cultures brought by migrants.
Back in Malaysia, Southe-ast Asian flavours naturally became part of that mix.
“And safe to say the direction is more like we want to make good food, without any limitation, without any box,” he said.
One of the items on the menu is a sea bass served with Ahmad’s take on romesco that incorporates green chilli and coconut milk.
Alongside it is a kerabu-like salad with mango and edamame, bringing another combination of influences to the plate.
He said the menu he planned focused on layering of flavours with Malaysian influences.
Aim said Gilda not only offers contemporary dining but is a neo bistro with items for brunch and small plates for customers who just want to hang out with their friends and family.
Gilda is open from Thursday to Monday from 11am to 4.30pm and 5.30pm to 10pm. Reservations can be made at https://gildadining.com.
3b153c8259f719bb: FARSTA, Sept 13 — “Good job!” Outside Stockholm’s Farsta subway station where a 2023 shooting killed two innocent bystanders, locals thank Max Akerwall and his police team for turning the tide on gang violence.
An otherwise tranquil country, Sweden has endured over a decade of brutal attacks by organised crime networks, featuring automatic weapons, grenades and explosives, sometimes in broad daylight.
An almost daily occurrence a few years ago as the networks battled over the drugs market, the violence has decreased significantly.
“Sweden was experiencing a wave of violence in 2022 and 2023,” said Akerwall, police commissioner for Stockholm’s southern district, recalling the peak of deadly shootings and bombings.
“But we’ve managed to reverse the trend,” he told AFP, the relief almost tangible in his voice.
In January-June this year, eight people were killed and 15 wounded in 39 shootings, down from 34 killed and 49 wounded in 205 shootings in the same period in 2022, according to police.
Bombings have come down from 108 in January-June last year to 75 this year.
Akerwall credits the turnaround to measures introduced by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing government, in power since 2022.
It has promised to pursue its crackdown if re-elected in Sunday’s general election.
The left-wing opposition is also in favour of maintaining the hard line.
“In the past four years we’ve gotten many new tools, with new legislation,” Akerwall said.

Tougher sentences for gun possession have been “a game changer”, he said, as have expanded police powers, new surveillance tools, broader international cooperation and more information-sharing between authorities.
‘Increased sense of security’
At a drab commercial centre in the nearby suburb of Ragsved – qualified by police as a high-crime “vulnerable area” with an “open drug scene” – cops on foot patrol watch out for known troublemakers.
Security cameras perched on building facades record every move.
“All of these measures help to create calm, an increased sense of security in society,” Akerwall said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Swedish police patrol a street outside the Farsta metro station in Farsta, south of Stockholm in a bid to quell a decade-long gang violence involving automatic weapons, grenades and explosives. — AFP pic
Greger Pettersson, a 65-year-old who has lived in Ragsved most of his life, said he had heard “several shootings” here in the past.
“I had a shooting right outside my home. That was pretty close.”
Yet he never felt unsafe enough to move away.
“You learn to read people” and stay out of the way, he said.
53-year-old Ahcene Oumeraci said the situation had improved.
“You don’t hear shootings anymore, there hasn’t been that much lately,” the father-of-five said.
Recruiting kids
But major challenges remain.

Gang leaders orchestrate operations from abroad, recruiting kids on encrypted apps to carry out hits for cash, knowing they won’t be prosecuted because they’re under the age of criminal responsibility, recently cut from 15 to 14.
“What still worries me is the recruiting. There are so unbelievably many young people being recruited on social media, on their phones,” Akerwall said.
From January to July, 170 children under the age of 15 were suspected of involvement in violent crimes, police data showed.

The government has introduced legislation requiring social media platforms to take down adverts for hitmen, abolished more lenient sentences for young offenders, and enabled police to use coercive measures against children to get at the criminals ordering the crimes.
It is also pursuing gang leaders hiding out abroad. The leader of the Foxtrot network, Rawa Majid, is known to be in Iran.
The networks have also infiltrated public agencies, politics, businesses and the legal and penitentiary systems, posing a “systemic threat,” Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer said.

Home to 10.6 million people, Sweden has more than 17,000 active gang criminals, police say. A half-million people live in areas with “parallel justice systems” run by the networks, a government inquiry concluded.
Sven Granath, criminology expert at Stockholm University, said Sweden needed to “safeguard its welfare system”.
“There will be fewer people inclined toward violence and criminal careers if society and the environment they grow up in is more secure.”
Akerwall is “hopeful,” saying: “We will do everything in our power to continue pushing back against crime.” — AFP
5f1def649a93e441: BRUSSELS, Sept 13 — Calls are growing louder in Europe for action against “pervert” smart glasses after secretly filmed footage of girls and women appeared online—with a petition in Britain demanding a ban on their sale.
Anyone wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant, with sales now hitting the millions.
The devices grabbed attention this summer after a marketing tie-up between Kylie Jenner, beauty mogul and member of the Kardashian dynasty, and tech giant Meta.
Since smartphones are now embedded in daily life, Big Tech is increasingly looking to glasses as the next big thing in wearable technology, helped by AI’s advances.
A 2013 push by Google failed to take off but Meta’s smart spectacles, developed in partnership with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, have fared much better.
Meta sold some seven million pairs in 2025, up from a total of two million in 2023 and 2024. Others, including Google and Snap, are also preparing to roll out AI-powered glasses.
But with exponential growth came the backlash.

Worries reached a peak in the summer in Europe, especially in Britain which saw intense media coverage of so-called “pervert glasses” alongisde reports that Meta is developing a facial recognition feature to be integrated into the devices.
In one case, a 17-year-old girl told British broadcaster Channel 4 News in August how she had been approached by a man who covertly recorded her and their interaction.
Contacted by AFP, Meta said it has taken multiple steps to prevent tampering with the blinking LED light intended to show other people the device is recording—a key concern of critics.
“These investments are already having a deterrent effect,” it said, saying companies offering to disable the LED lights had shut down as a result.
EU ‘must act’
In the meantime, Norway’s capital Oslo banned the glasses in schools this week as the government mulls regulating their use and considers a ban on features that enable facial recognition in public.
There are similar calls for the European Union to take up the issue, while France’s CNIL data protection watchdog has urged “vigilance”.
A Swedish designer, Mateusz Pozar, launched a “Ban Ray” site earlier this year, providing signs to ban smart glasses from venues and selling stickers.
Pozar said he started the site after his girlfriend was approached by two men wearing the glasses and recording her, which “freaked her out”.

He said he wanted a discussion about how “we as a society feel about this technology” before it becomes ubiquitous. “This is a lever to have a discussion about privacy, personal rights, control over my data.”
Pozar also pointed to his concerns about data extraction after reports about Kenya-based workers who reviewed graphic content captured by Meta’s AI glasses.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer Gen 2 smart glasses on display at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, Spain on March 5, 2026, featuring a 12MP camera, 3K video, and built-in Meta AI. — AFP pic

EU lawmaker Veronika Cifrova Ostrihonova told AFP she raised the issue with the bloc’s executive after the first cases of women being secretly filmed, seeking to know if the glasses comply with data protection and AI rules.
“I am still awaiting an answer,” the Slovak lawmaker said.
“We need clear EU rules to protect and strong enforcement to make sure new technologies don’t come at the expense of our fundamental rights,” she said.
The European Commission said national data protection authorities were “responsible for monitoring and enforcing” privacy rules.

The EU executive would not be drawn on what further action it could take, but the independent European Data Protection Board commissioned a report expected in autumn looking at the glasses’ “social acceptability”.
Consent issues
That report will guide the European Parliament, where lawmaker Alex Agius Saliba said there were concerns across the political spectrum.
“We must act as soon as possible,” he said.
“For me, they are still ‘pervert glasses’,” Saliba said. “As things stand today, we should definitely go for a ban” until they’re proven safe.
A “Stop Smart Glasses” campaign launched in Britain and Ireland, with a petition and call for supporters to contact stores to stop their sale.
The petition has more than 9,100 signatures so far. The British government must respond if it reaches 10,000.

One of the campaign’s founders, teacher Guy Holder, said he had several concerns about the glasses including their effects on girls and women and a broader “invasion” of public spaces that could lead to “total surveillance”.
“We are also concerned more broadly about an atmosphere in which it feels like anybody can film anybody without their knowledge or consent,” he told AFP. — AFP
9c0d1c4e7082a308: GENAPPE, Sept 13 — Perched atop a larch tree, Luca Bruscia, a sporty 25-year-old pruner, collects pine cones that Belgian authorities hope will help strengthen the country’s forests in the face of a changing climate.

The cones’ seeds will be planted in other woody corners of the European nation to boost tree diversity and resilience — an effort that gained more urgency this year after Belgium was ravaged by its largest wildfire in a century.
“We used to see this kind of thing happen in southern Europe, and now it’s happening here. It’s quite striking,” Bruscia’s boss Adrien Baudoin said of fires and prolonged spells of dry weather.
“It’s going to get worse and worse,” he added. “We have no choice but to adapt.”
Bruscia was one of four forestry workers taking part in the annual high-altitude cone harvest on a September morning in the Bois D’Hez woodland in Genappe south of Brussels.
It took the team a few attempts with a tool resembling a giant slingshot to secure throw-lines on high sturdy branches of several tall trees.
They then climbed up about 40 metres (130 feet) and spent a couple of hours on each tree, collecting several kilogrammes of cones in canvas bags.
The harvest is carried out from mid-August to mid-September, before the pine cones open up, releasing their seeds into the wind.
Once collected, the cones are handed to the forestry office of Marche-en-Famenne, about 80 kilometres (50 miles) southeast of Genappe.
They are dried and then placed in a washing-machine-like spinner to extract the seeds.
‘Long-term view’
After meticulous sorting, checks and a spell in cold storage sometimes lasting years, the office sells them on for planting in Belgium’s public and private forests.
A kilogramme – equivalent to some 35,000 seeds – costs about €3,400 (RM15,900), with a germination rate of up to 50 per cent.
“The forest of the future will be highly diverse,” said the office’s head Eleonore Scholzen, whose goal is to prepare local woods for the next 200 years.
With global warming “we need to take a very long-term view” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A forested area scorched following a wildfire in the Hautes Fagnes (High Fens) nature reserve near Baraque Michel, eastern Belgium on September 9, 2026. The fire mushroomed to half the size of Manhattan – 3,000 hectares – charring a huge expanse of peatland, pine trees and hiking trails. — AFP pic
Dominated by spruce trees, Belgian forests have suffered as the lack of arboreal diversity has caused soil acidification and left trees more vulnerable to insects, diseases and natural disasters.
With global warming bringing about more frequent and intense extreme weather events, Belgium’s nature and forestry department is pushing for diversification.

From sycamores to maples, a variety of tree species, some once found mainly in southern Europe, are being planted around the country in the hope they will make local woods better equipped to withstand rising temperatures.

“Trees migrate naturally, but this migration is not fast enough to keep pace with climate change,” said Scholzen, who was among the responders to the massive fire in the High Fens nature reserve in August, explaining the need for a human boost. — AFP
892567a6cccd87d5: GUA MUSANG, Sept 13 — Lipstick and face powder may have replaced charcoal and limestone paste in the beauty routines of the Orang Asli from the Temiar tribe, but modernisation has not erased the centuries-old tradition of facial adornment passed down through generations.

Endah Angah, 37, said the practice of painting geometric motifs, including long and wavy lines and dots, on the face remained deeply cherished by her community as an enduring symbol of its cultural heritage.

She said the growing difficulty of sourcing traditional beauty ingredients such as kesumba seeds had led her community to increasingly rely on modern cosmetics, which were easier to obtain than having to venture into the forest in search of the natural materials.
“In the past, these natural ingredients were easy to find, so we didn’t have to go deep into the forest to look for them. But now, they’re getting harder to find.

“Using modern cosmetics is much easier for us. The red and black colours from lipstick and eyeliner also make the patterns on our faces look neater and brighter, and they last longer too,” the housewife told Bernama recently.
Rahimah Punai, 39, said modern cosmetics might have changed the way the facial motifs were created, but their spiritual meaning and connection to their ancestral heritage remained intact.

“We make sure every horizontal and wavy line, as well as every dot, is drawn carefully because each one has its own meaning. The lines represent the river, while the dots symbolise our connection to nature.

“Nothing has changed, except that we now use modern cosmetics. We have to follow what our ancestors passed down to us and keep it the same to preserve our customs and heritage. So, we cannot just add streaks to the forehead, nose or cheeks,” she said.
Abong Busu, 55, said the custom remained deeply rooted among the Temiar tribe and continued to be practised during religious ceremonies such as the sewang and at community gatherings.
“This is how we introduce the tradition to the younger generation. The children are very interested and often ask us a lot of questions about it,” she said.

Meanwhile, Kelantan State Department for Culture and Arts (JKKN) director Rohaniza Abdullah said the use of modern cosmetics, while retaining the original facial motifs, represented a new way of preserving and continuing the traditional heritage practice.

She said creativity in producing modern-style facial decorations was a way to keep the heritage relevant while preserving its originality and aesthetic value as an important part of Orang Asli identity and socio-cultural life.

“The use of modern cosmetics is a positive development for the community because the traditional facial motifs can still be recreated while retaining their original patterns and colours. This also helps preserve the tradition for future generations.
“Preserving this tradition for the next generation is important, so efforts by various parties, especially to engage young people, must continue,” she said.
Rohaniza added that the uniqueness and symbolism behind the facial motifs could make the traditional art an iconic representation of Orang Asli culture. — Bernama
211c10b3c1e24c8c: KUALA LUMPUR: History is everywhere in Melaka, from centuries-old temples and churches to heritage buildings that tell stories of its colourful past.

But tucked amidst the bustle of the city is a place whose significance many may not know. It is the ancestral home of Tan Cheng Lock, the statesman and nation builder who founded MCA and became a leading voice for Malaya’s Chinese community.

A firm believer in a united, multiracial Malaya, Cheng Lock championed equal citizenship and cooperation among the country’s different communities, helping lay the foundations for the nation that would emerge.
Located on 111 Jalan Tan Cheng Lock, formerly Heeren Street, the house remains in the care of his descendants, who continue to preserve it as an important part of the family’s heritage.
According to Cheng Lock's granddaughter, Tan Siok Choo, the house dates back to 1799 and was purchased by her great-great-grandfather, Tan Choon Bock, for use as the family home in 1875.

Cheng Lock lived there, while Siok Choo grew up in nearby Klebang Besar and visited about once a week. She did not enjoy these visits much as a child, as getting there meant a 45-minute journey along winding roads crowded with bullock carts.
“We also never really got to see my grandparents very much. I only gained more appreciation for the house later in life, when I was writing a book on it,” Siok Choo, 73, told FMT Lifestyle.

From the outside, the home resembles a traditional Melaka shophouse. Above its main gate hang two paper lanterns emblazoned with the Tan family name, which Siok Choo noted also carry a message about the importance of education.
“The lanterns say, 'If you don’t educate your son, you have a donkey. If you don’t educate your daughter, you have a pig',” she said.
“I was very impressed by how enlightened the person who created these lanterns was, especially in placing such importance on educating women, which was certainly not the norm at the time."
The message appears very much in keeping with the late Cheng Lock’s progressive views on women’s equality.

One of the most striking things about the house is its sheer length, stretching across three courtyards. At the heart of the central courtyard stands a towering tree which, according to Siok Choo, was planted during her grandfather’s time and continues to flourish today.

According to Siok Choo, the house also played a part in the country’s political history, with Tunku Abdul Rahman holding meetings there with Chinese educationists to discuss the future direction of education in Malaya.

Her favourite part of the house is the first hall. Taking pride of place is an ornate altar dedicated to Guan Yu, beneath a sign bearing the Chinese characters for “Spirit of Righteousness”. Also displayed there are several statues of Guan Yu, as well as Kuan Yin, the goddess of mercy.
“In the altar, we have enshrined the family values of righteousness, loyalty and integrity, mercy and compassion,” Siok Choo said.
Its walls are also adorned with reproductions of essays written by the noted Song Dynasty poet Su Dongpo, known for building the famous “Pavilion of Timely Rain” in China.

The house’s second hall, known as the Hall of Filial Remembrance, contains another altar where Siok Choo conducts Confucian ancestor-remembrance rituals. She also offers fruit and Peranakan food at the altar.
“A lot of Chinese don’t have ancestral homes any more, so I think the ancestral remembrance ceremonies are slowly dying out. That's quite a pity,” she said.
The rooms of the house are filled with photographs, documents and personal mementoes chronicling generations of the Tan family.

Hanging in the study where Cheng Lock once wrote his speeches, for example, is a rare photograph of Sultan Ibrahim Al-Masyhur of Johor with his last wife and daughter. The photograph is inscribed with Cheng Lock’s name and was personally sent to him.
The house’s upper floor contains the bridal chamber, as well as a bedroom where former prime minister Tunku Abdul Rahman would stay whenever he visited Cheng Lock.
Siok Choo also pointed out a four-poster bed which, according to Tunku Abdul Rahman’s memoirs, was rather uncomfortable to sleep in.
Tunku, however, was apparently too kind-hearted to ever tell her grandfather about it.

Maintaining the family home over the years has been a challenging and resource-intensive task. Siok Choo recalled that during the pandemic, the house went largely unattended for three years, resulting in the deterioration of many items within.
Despite these challenges, she remains deeply attached to her family's ancestral home and hopes it will be preserved for future generations.
“It's more than just a house; it really shaped my grandfather and the rest of my relatives by instilling in them values that influenced their views on life and family.
“I think that’s important, and I hope it will one day be passed down to my nephews and niece.”
abc300255c4a0538: KUALA LUMPUR: Akar umbi Umno menyambut baik kemungkinan kerjasama dengan PAS, namun mengingatkan pucuk pimpinan supaya tidak mengulangi pengalaman Muafakat Nasional (MN) yang 'mengecewakan'.

Ketua Penerangan Umno Klang, Wan Mohamad Yusoff Wan Abdullah, berkata kerjasama dengan PAS perlu dibuat dengan berhati-hati kerana masih wujud kebimbangan dalam kalangan akar umbi terhadap 'kesetiaan' PAS.
"Jangan PAS mainkan kita. Kita dah pernah kena dalam MN. Menangis-nangis. Dalam dewan ramai yang sedih. Pemimpin kena berhati-hatilah. Kami harapkan.
"Masih ada rasa kebimbangan dalam kalangan akar umbi," katanya ketika ditemui FMT pada Perhimpunan Agung Umno di Pusat Dagangan Dunia Kuala Lumpur, semalam.

Wan Mohamad mengulas usaha mengeratkan hubungan antara Umno dan PAS, berlatarkan cakap-cakap mengenai penjajaran semula politik antara Barisan Nasional dan PAS serta sekutunya dalam PN, susulan gandingan pada PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan.

Muafakat Nasional yang ditubuhkan Umno dan PAS pada Sept 2019 terkubur selepas PAS membentuk Perikatan Nasional bersama Bersatu, dan pada masa yang sama mahu Bersatu diterima dalam MN tetapi dibantah Umno.

Pada 9 Sept lalu, Timbalan Presiden Umno Mohamad Hasan berkata Umno tidak mahu lagi 'dipermainkan' dalam usaha penyatuan politik Melayu-Islam dan akan lebih berhati-hati terhadap sebarang kerjasama pada masa depan.
Ahli Jawatankuasa Umno Tenggara, Ahmad Sapari, berkata akar umbi secara umumnya tidak mempunyai masalah dengan usaha menyatukan parti-parti Melayu demi kepentingan bersama.
Beliau bagaimanapun mengingatkan Umno supaya meneliti sebarang syarat sebelum menerima kerjasama dengan PAS.
"Takut pisang berbuah dua kali. Kena lihat syarat dia. Kena teliti syarat," katanya.
Ahli Jawatankuasa Umno Gopeng, Isa Ulong, pula berkata kerjasama dengan PAS hanya boleh dipertimbangkan jika terdapat mekanisme yang benar-benar dapat mengukuhkan persefahaman.
"Kalau ada kerjasama kena ada yang mengukuh, kena ada sesuatu yang perlu dipegang," katanya.
Pada masa sama, Isa berpandangan Umno kini mempunyai ruang untuk bangkit semula, dan tidak seharusnya menganggap PAS sebagai satu-satunya penentu kekuatan politik Melayu.
Naib Ketua Umno Klang, Sheikh Rajesh Sheikh Ahmad, melihat keterbukaan terhadap kerjasama dengan PAS sebagai permulaan yang baik selepas sekian lama diimpikan oleh penyokong parti Melayu.
Ditanya adakah Umno perlu berhati-hati, Sheikh Rajesh berkata kelancaran kerjasama itu bergantung kepada usaha pihak atasan menyelesaikan masalah mereka.
"Kalau atasan tak dapat selesaikan masalah, yang di bawah ini nak kerja agak susah," katanya.
5715c82c84cf543f: Last week, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent launched an “economic D-Day” programme, intended to cut Iran off from all trading partners. So far, this intensified economic blockade has only contributed to an escalation of the US-Iran war, rather than moving it towards a conclusion.
That probably will not change, because China is unwilling to cooperate. And this is the reality that US policymakers must now face: Most possible paths to lasting peace run through China.

Wars end because one side gives up, or because influential people on both sides grow tired of the losses and want to move on, or because a powerful third party imposes peace. Seen through this lens, the US-Iran conflict could last for a long time.

Hardliners on both sides are now deeply entrenched. Iran is not about to surrender, the US will not risk a full-scale invasion, and China, the only third party with enough clout to make a difference, seems inclined just to watch. Bessent’s economic isolation campaign is unlikely to prove decisive without the support of Iran’s most important trading partner.

If China continues to do business with Iran, the current Iranian leadership will most likely survive. Any US threats against China remain non-credible, given China’s leverage over the supply of critical minerals needed by the sectors driving economic growth in the US and other major countries. No critical minerals means no computer chips—and no AI-led investment boom for the US.
Iran and the US agreed to a ceasefire in June, and this was quickly followed by a memorandum of understanding (MoU). But none of this has led to real peace.

Iran is still effectively limiting passage through the Strait of Hormuz, and the US is still turning away most vessels associated with Iran. The MoU looked good on paper, but it was never fully implemented by either side.

When the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, and Iran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz, some strategic thinkers believed that China would press for a quick resolution of the conflict, primarily because, until recently, as much as 60% of its oil imports passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
But this turned out to be a miscalculation. China had more than 1.2 billion barrels—200 million above its usual reserves—when the conflict began, and still holds more than 1.15 billion barrels today.
At the same time, the disruption and increase in global oil prices have accelerated demand for renewables and electric vehicles, which has helped China’s exports.
Ironically, these sectors are the same ones in which China has huge excess capacity. In that sense, the current crisis has postponed the financial losses in these sectors.

Overall, China turned out to be one of the least sensitive countries to the current crisis. This should be an important consideration in any future calculations by US policymakers and rules out instability in the Middle East as part of the toolkit for containing China.
The main loser from this war is the broader Middle East. The world economy is learning how to survive with oil and gas exports from the region at around half of their prewar level.

Of course, it is a relatively costly adjustment, but the longer this crisis continues, the less sensitive the world economy may become to disruptions in the Middle East. This may not be good news for the region’s oil-exporting countries, and they are likely to lose market share over the medium term.
Countries in the region, especially Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar, have also learned that reliance on US security may not work as well as they thought.

Saudi Arabia is trying to increase its reliance on other regional allies, while Qatar and the UAE are talking directly with Iran and using economic incentives to buy some security for themselves. These shifts support the argument that regional economic integration must be part of the solution to the current impasse.
At first glance, more diplomacy by regional players may strengthen the case for the US washing its hands of the issue and leaving the problem to Iran’s neighbours.

But it is very hard to see how the nuclear issue would be addressed in this scenario, and without addressing that concern about Iran, it may be very hard to make any long-term plans or even achieve partial economic integration in the region.

The only stable solution to this crisis is one that involves China and increases economic integration in the region, as well as addressing the nuclear issue by integrating Iran’s programme into a regional civilian electricity production supply chain led by China.

Chinese president Xi Jinping is due to visit Washington at the end of September. Perhaps the US-Iran conflict can be resolved in the context of a broader discussion with President Donald Trump. Or perhaps China will be content to watch and wait.

Simon Johnson, a 2024 Nobel laureate in economics and a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, is a professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management. Amir Kermani, professor of finance and real estate at the Haas School of Business at the University of California, Berkeley, is a research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research.
The views expressed are those of the writers and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
09cc2c34b099d858: NEW YORK: Elena Rybakina denied Aryna Sabalenka a third straight US Open title on Saturday, punctuating her rise to world number one with a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory over the player she's replacing at the summit.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina, assured of supplanting Sabalenka atop the rankings by reaching the semi-finals in New York, won her third Grand Slam title to go with her 2022 Wimbledon crown and the Australian Open trophy she lifted this year with a win over Sabalenka.
Rybakina has played three of her four Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, winning two and losing one, at the 2023 Australian Open.
"I can't find the words now," Rybakina said as she accepted the trophy at a tournament where she had never before made it past the fourth round. "I'm falling more and more in love with New York."
Sabalenka, unbeaten in 20 prior matches at Flushing Meadows, clawed back courageously in the second set, breaking Rybakina for the first time in the final game to force the third.
But with her trademark aplomb, Rybakina roared back to finish off a frustrated Sabalenka, who smashed her racket while sitting in her chair as her opponent was applauded by the crowd.
Sabalenka, 28, will end the year without a major title for the first time since 2022.

The two biggest hitters in the women's game came out swinging. After Rybakina held to love in the second game, she had Sabalenka in trouble in the third, unleashing a backhand passing winner to set up the first break chances of the match.

Sabalenka saved one break point with a forehand down the line and ripped another forehand winner on the next. A double fault gave Rybakina another look but Sabalenka held on with a volley winner before sealing the game with her first ace.

Two games later, however, Rybakina seized control as she relentlessly pushed Sabalenka back with her deep groundstrokes. Unsettled, Sabalenka double faulted on break point, then smacked a ball skyward to draw a code violation warning for ball abuse.
After another love hold from Rybakina, and a break point saved from Sabalenka, the margin was 4-3.
Rybakina hadn't committed a single unforced error through seven games and Sabalenka was looking increasingly desperate.
Serving to extend the set at 5-3, she crushed an overhead several feet beyond the baseline and had to regroup before closing the game with an ace and a service winner.

But Rybakina wouldn't be denied, and despite a hint of nerves as she coughed up her first double fault of the match, she polished off the set 6-4 with a screaming backhand winner before Sabalenka sailed a shot long to end the deciding rally.
'I guess next year'
The second set started much the same, Sabalenka saving a pair of break points in the third game before thumping down a massive serve to hold.
She had yet to make any headway against Rybakina's serve, but she seemed to have found something on her own, twice holding to love as she took a 5-4 lead.

Sabalenka's first break points of the match gave her a chance to close out the set, but she smacked a forehand long on the first and belted a service return long on the second as Rybakina leveled the set at 5-5.
Nevertheless, Sabalenka was gaining in confidence. She held for a 6-5 lead then broke Rybakina with authority to force a third set -- but it proved only a brief reprieve.
"I wish I could have performed a little better," Sabalenka told the Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd, her voice breaking, "but I guess next year."
833882561935c705: NEW DELHI: Members of the 11-nation BRICS group including China, Russia, Iran and India called for calm in the Middle East at a summit in New Delhi on Saturday, overcoming earlier divisions to issue a joint statement.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who joined Russian, Iranian, Indian and other leaders in India's capital, told the summit that the Middle East war "does not serve the common interests of the international community."

Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping had failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Feb 28.

But leaders issued a statement on Saturday after intense diplomatic efforts by host India, as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.

"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia," the joint statement said, adding the countries "call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation."
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

"We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders as he opened the two-day summit.
Modi said BRICS nations "represent 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and more than 25 per cent of global trade."
But finding balance in the bloc is a tough diplomatic task.
India maintains cordial relations with both Iran and US ally Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

Iran's Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a "regional policeman", with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Pezeshkian met with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the summit sidelines.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. The Russian president, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
- 'HANDLING DIFFERENCES' -
Xi's participation is also being closely watched because it is his first visit to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.

"Although our two countries are different in many respects, they are fully capable of complementing each other's strengths, supporting one another, achieving mutual success and advancing together," Xi said as he met Modi, in a video released from New Delhi.

His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along the disputed Tibetan border between China and India, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500km high-altitude border.
India's foreign ministry said in a statement after the meeting that "the two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question."
Modi "underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border related issues," the foreign ministry added.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.

"Both sides should... work hand-in-hand to promote high-quality major financial cooperation, advocate an equal and sustainable global order, and foster an economic globalisation that is open and inclusive," Xi said.

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday – exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 – waving placards against Xi's visit.--AFP

66d24e9c1ac07200: NEW DELHI: India and China's leaders pledged on Saturday to build up business and transport links, New Delhi said, as both rebuild ties badly damaged by a 2020 military clash on their disputed Himalayan border.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping met on the sidelines of a summit of the BRICS group of emerging nations in New Delhi — Xi's first trip to India in seven years.
Military tensions have eased, but businesses in both countries say they continue to face hurdles, including red tape, visa delays and restrictions on selling industrial equipment.
"The two leaders ... underscored the need to further promote cultural exchanges, business linkages and greater mobility between the two countries," the Indian foreign ministry said in a statement.

"On economic and trade relations, they underlined the need to address each other's concerns, including structural trade imbalance and supply chain issues, and facilitation of meaningful and predictable market access," it said.
Bilateral trade reached a record US$155.6 billion in 2025, according to Chinese customs data.

China has become India's largest source of imports, with Indian purchases from China rising to about US$132 billion in the 2025/26 fiscal year. India's exports to China remain much smaller, leaving New Delhi with a trade deficit of more than US$100 billion.
Xi said China has always viewed and developed China-India relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
Institutional exchanges between the two countries are gradually being restored, the list of areas for cooperation is growing and bilateral trade has reached a new high, Xi said according to Xinhua.
China and India fought a brief but brutal border war in 1962, and their relationship soured again after the 2020 border skirmish killed 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers.
Ties began recovering at the end of 2024 after Xi and Modi agreed to end their military stand-off in the western Himalayas.
Irritants remain as both countries continue to maintain substantial military deployments in the Himalayas and border talks make slow progress.
Modi said that peace in the border areas remained an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations, according to the Indian statement.
The nuclear-armed neighbours share a roughly 3,800km, largely unmarkedfrontier.--REUTERS
d373ffffdaaafd7c: MISANO ADRIATICO: MotoGP world champion Marc Marquez led almost all the way to win the San Marino Grand Prix sprint race on Saturday ahead of his Aprilia rivals.

The Ducati star beat his two main world title challengers, both riding Aprilias, finishing 1.068sec ahead of Italian Marco Bezzecchi, with fellow Spaniard Jorge Martin crossing third in northern Italy.
Bezzecchi had started from pole position after setting a Misano track record in qualifying, but Marquez got off to a better start and overtook on the inside at the first corner.
From there on it was a dominant display for Marquez who is targeting his eighth top-class championship and his 10th overall.
At the controls of his factory Ducati, the 33-year-old had a one-second lead over his rivals after five laps.
Bezzecchi fought back and managed to close the gap slightly but had no real chance of catching up to the older of the Marquez brothers.
Championship leader Martin, starting from the second row, moved into third place halfway through the 13-lap race.
The battle for the riders' title is heating up among the three contenders, with Martin 14 points ahead of Marquez and Bezzecchi 22 points off the leader.
On Sunday, Marquez is looking to repeat his success at the Aragon GP where he won both races, against a "very fast Marco (Bezzecchi)" who had started from pole.
"Same tyre as in Aragon, same strategy as in Aragon," said Marquez, who explained his choice of a medium rear tyre had helped contain Bezzecchi's aggression on soft tyres.
"Marco will be the man to beat (on Sunday). He has something extra; he’s going to attack."
"We saw today that he never gives up."
Bezzecchi is targeting his first MotoGP world title this year after finishing third last season.
"Overall it was a good day," said Bezzecchi.
"At the end, when I got confidence, I started to go faster and because of this, I'm very happy."
54fa71305ce9b67a: PARIS: Celine Dion wept tears of joy on Saturday as she fulfilled her dream of returning to the stage after years battling a rare neurological disorder, with a sell-out concert in Paris.

The 58-year-old French Canadian singer appeared visibly moved as she opened her first full concert in six years with her 1990s French-language ballad "On ne change pas" ("One Doesn't Change"), singing to a crowd of 30,000 enthralled fans that one newspaper said included US former first lady Michelle Obama.
"These are, of course, tears of joy. I'm so delighted to see you," Dion said, blowing kisses to the audience at the packed Plenitude Arena on the western edge of Paris.

Her return to the stage underscored a remarkable comeback after Stiff Person Syndrome, an incurable condition that causes stiffness and cramps, forced her to cancel shows and cast years of uncertainty over whether she would ever perform again.
"The path was rockier than expected," she said, speaking in French and English.
"But I held on to a faint ray of light in the distance, deep in the mountains."
"Tonight, I want to sing for you, sing for myself, sing for life," she added.
- 'UNREAL' -
The largely female crowd sported sequined dresses and tops, glittered cheeks, and T-shirts emblazoned with the star's image or nods to her biggest hits.
"It's unreal to be here!," said Elisabeth Landry, a 38-year-old Quebecer who lives near the star's hometown of Charlemagne.
"I was convinced we'd never see her again, especially not embarking on a run of concerts like this."
French daily Le Parisien said the former first lady of the United States was "discreetly attending this first concert."
Just hours before, one of the best-selling singers of all time greeted admirers outside her luxury hotel a short walk from the Arc de Triomphe.
Albertina Cabral, a fan from the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo, said she could barely put her feelings into words.
"It's unbelievable to stay here and to go to the concert and to see Celine so close," she said. "And she's feeling good, she's happy."
Paris spared no effort in welcoming Dion, drawing thousands of fans from across the world, including some who flew in from as far away as the French Polynesian island of Tahiti.
For days, Paris played host to costume contests, giant karaoke parties and tribute cruises on the Seine.

On Friday, the iconic cauldron rose above the Tuileries Garden, echoing the diva's surprise appearance up the Eiffel Tower to perform "Hymn to Love" by Edith Piaf during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics in 2024.
A lyric from the song, "I'd go and fetch the moon if you asked me to", along with the singer's first name, was projected in big letters onto the balloon.
The suburban train station serving the arena has been temporarily renamed "Celine."
- 'A LEGEND' -
Chloe and Katy Rydquist, who travelled from London, had spent around £1,500 (US$2,000) on their tickets, saying Dion's return to the stage justified the cost.
"She's a legend," said Chloe.
The star's residency is projected to generate hundreds of millions of euros in economic benefits.
She kicks off her 26-date run with 16 sold-out shows in September and October, before returning for another 10 in May.
Fans who missed out on tickets have found other ways to catch a glimpse of their idol.
Dion has regularly stepped outside the Royal Monceau hotel to greet waiting fans, at times breaking into song and dance with them well into the early hours.
Over her four-decade career, Dion has sold around 260 million albums in English and French, with hits including "It's All Coming Back to Me Now" and "Because You Loved Me."
Dion revealed in late 2022 that she had been diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome, an autoimmune condition that can cause severe muscle stiffness and agonising spasms.
Dion has described it as making her feel as though she is being strangled, with cramps so intense they have left her with broken ribs.
She has returned to stage after what she has described as years of training "like an athlete", doing ballet and pilates several times a week, as well as voice therapy.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd
bcb7a0c212a81804: LONDON: Tottenham were booed off after their goalless start to the Premier League season stretched to a fourth match following Saturday's dismal 0-0 draw against Everton.
Roberto De Zerbi's expensively assembled side have made a wretched opening to the new campaign and they were easily held by Everton in north London.
Tottenham have taken two points from their first four matches, with their only goals this season coming against second tier Charlton in the League Cup.

72fff2ccc2b33052: DOONBEG, Ireland: Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love to see" a united Ireland, wading into a politically sensitive subject as he embarked on a two-day Irish visit that blurs the lines between his presidency and personal business interests.
After meeting Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland – split for over a century – would be "a fantastic thing."
"It's going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now," he told reporters, adding "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously."
The island of Ireland has been split between the Irish republic in the south and Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, since 1921.

Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland that killed about 3,000 people, a referendum can be held if the UK government determines a majority there is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.
Republic of Ireland voters would also have to endorse reunification in a poll for it to happen.
The United States has previously adopted a neutral position on the issue.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted last month that a unity referendum was "off the table", drawing a sharp response from the pro-unity party Sinn Fein.

Asked about Trump's comments, a spokesperson for his Downing Street office referred reporters to comments Burnham made in parliament Wednesday when he vowed to "stick to the Good Friday Agreement 100 per cent."
However Gavin Robinson, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said on X that "as unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic."
- DIVERGENCES -

Trump had touched down at Dublin airport shortly before 8.25am (0725 GMT) under a security operation dubbed one of the largest ever mounted in Ireland and reportedly costing 20 million euros (US$23 million).
At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, have been mobilised.

In Dublin, at least 2,000 protesters waving Palestinian flags and holding placards rallied Saturday lunchtime against the president's visit, chanting "Donald Trump's not welcome here", AFP reporters saw.
One sign read "no imperialists in Ireland" while some held explicit inflatable balloons showing Trump in sex acts with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Trump is a warmonger," student Cillian Whelan, 19, told AFP. "He has no right to be in my country. He should be on trial."
One small group of demonstrators – dressed in black and wearing masks and dark glasses – set a US flag on fire, according to The Irish Times.

Smaller protests also occurred at Shannon Airport, where the US leader transited, and in Doonbeg on Ireland's west coast, where the Trump Organization's 2014-purchased course is hosting golf's Irish Open tournament.
Police said three women – aged in their 20s, 30s and 40s – had appeared in a western Irish court late Saturday after being arrested for separate trespass and public order offences there.

After completing engagements in Dublin, Trump made a dramatic landing in Doonbeg aboard Marine One, and was soon photographed watching over the 18th green during the third round of the Open flanked by his sons Don Jr. and Eric.
He was reportedly given a rapturous reception during a brief appearance in the resort's members' bar, with drinkers chanting "USA."
- 'STRONG VIEW' -
Earlier in Dublin, Trump appeared to receive a frostier reception from left-wing President Catherine Connolly, an outspoken critic of the US leader.
"I conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted," Connolly said in a post-meeting statement.
He then met Martin, when the Iran war and US tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals and immigration were on the agenda.
Ireland and the United States have long been close allies, partly because of their common ancestral ties.
But the Irish government's politics diverge sharply from those of the Trump administration on many issues, with Ireland being one of Europe's most pro-Palestinian countries.
It is among several countries, including Spain, the UK and France, that have announced a trade ban targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In Doonbeg, some 40,000 fans are expected at the Open over the weekend. Trump may even award the trophy Sunday.
The 80-year-old golf-mad president has promoted his family's courses and other businesses unabashedly since returning to the White House for his second presidential stint in January 2025.
Trinity College Dublin US history professor Daniel Gear told AFP that Trump "sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president."--AFP

defb6abd419a669e: KYIV: US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and special envoy Jared Kushner said this weekend that he hoped to announce the "next steps" of talks to end the Ukraine war within a "couple of weeks".

e7a2f12a626c10b2: Hull hold Chelsea, Liverpool fail to beat Fulham in Premier League
AFP
LONDON: Hull held free-scoring Chelsea 2-2 at Stamford Bridge to go third in the Premier League as Liverpool failed to find a way past struggling Fulham in a 0-0 draw on Saturday.
It was a familiar tale for Chelsea as the front three of Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer dazzled, but the Blues were undone by an inability to defend.
In five games against top-flight opposition since Xabi Alonso took charge, Chelsea have scored 16 times and conceded 12.
Hull were the last side in the Premier League to concede, but after three clean sheets they were finally breached when Rogers drilled in at the near post on seven minutes.
Mohamed Belloumi took advantage of Chelsea's slackness at the back to blast home on the volley after Jorrel Hato got caught under a cross to the back post.
The Algerian winger then put Hull in front with a deflected strike after Emi Martinez failed to deal with a corner.
Pedro drilled a Palmer cross into the top corner to bring Chelsea level just after the hour mark.
But the home side could not find a winner as Hull's honeymoon back in the Premier League goes on with only defending champions Arsenal and Manchester City above them in the table.
- FULHAM FIGHT FOR ARBELOA -
Liverpool remain unbeaten under Andoni Iraola but there were boos at Anfield after Fulham picked up their first point under Alvaro Arbeloa.
Former Liverpool defender Arbeloa was reportedly fighting for his job after losing his first three league matches since arriving in west London from Real Madrid.
Yet a Liverpool forward line featuring three £100 million (US$135 million) players in Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak failed to click against the Cottagers' leaky defence.

Indeed it was Fulham who had the better chances to take all three points as Gonzalo Garcia missed a glorious opportunity in the first half and Alisson Becker produced a brilliant save to deny Josh King the winner.
Liverpool climb to sixth but could find themselves already six points off the top should Arsenal win at Sunderland later on Saturday.
Aston Villa are rooted in the relegation zone after Nottingham Forest exacted revenge with a 2-1 win at Villa Park.
Villa beat their Midlands rivals in the Europa League semi-finals last season on their way to lifting a first trophy for 30 years.
Many eyebrows were raised at the club record reported £45 million Forest paid Chelsea for Liam Delap after failing to make the grade at Stamford Bridge.
But Delap proved his worth with a long-range strike into the bottom corner to open the scoring.
Alysson levelled with Villa's first league goal of the season, but Igor Jesus secured Oliver Glasner's first win as Forest boss.
Glasner's old club Crystal Palace's poor start to the campaign continued with a 3-2 home defeat to Ipswich.
The visitors were aided by Axel Disasi's first half red card as Zian Flemming's first goal for the Tractor Boys snatched all three points in stoppage time.
Brentford remain unbeaten thanks to Kevin Schade's double in a 2-2 draw at Bournemouth.
The Cherries, by contrast, are yet to win in the Premier League under Marco Rose despite leading in all four games.
Tottenham are aiming to kickstart their league season with a first goal and win at home to Everton later.
Manchester United host local rivals City in the pick of Sunday's action.

9f228d8d08f8675c: Nvidia spent a whopping $20 billion late last year to license Groq’s AI accelerator tech and hire away key members of its engineering team in an everything-but-the-kitchen-sink deal. The acquihire technically left Groq’s core inference-as-a-service business intact, but was clearly architected in such a way as to fly under regulators' radar. Only it didn’t. This week, The New York Times reported that the US Department of Justice had launched an antitrust probe into the deal. It’s hard to argue that Nvidia didn’t strip the startup for parts. It may not have been a merger in the traditional sense, but without its engineering staff, Groq may as well be Nvidia’s puppet at this point. Despite this, Nvidia contends the deal is a great American success story. “The Groq story is a prime example of the American system working as designed to promote innovation, reward entrepreneurs, and benefit consumers. The law is designed to encourage America's startup ecosystem and promote the fundamental rights of inventors and workers to pursue their dreams,” an Nvidia statement provided to El Reg and other media reads. Whether the acquihire of Groq actually harmed competition is another matter entirely. But, even if the Justice Department did force Nvidia to unwind the team, it’s probably too late. What exactly did Nvidia buy? Nvidia’s Groq acquihire bought it two key assets: mature silicon and the talent necessary to continue its development. Groq – which, by the way, is completely unrelated to Elon Musk’s Grok model series – made a name for itself using SRAM-heavy dataflow accelerators to speed up LLM inference to hundreds and now thousands of tokens a second, something that GPU-based systems from Nvidia had struggled to do on their own. But while faster than GPUs, the accelerators couldn’t achieve rapid throughput. Think of it this way: If Groq’s LPUs were the F1 cars, Nvidia’s GPUs were more like a city bus. But combine the two and you get something more akin to a sport pickup. At GTC in March, Nvidia unveiled its LPX racks, which are powered by 256 Groq-3 accelerators. As we understand it, they are really lightly modified versions of the startup’s existing Groq-2 chip designs, which makes sense, because three months is absurdly fast to tape out new silicon. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang promised Groq-3 combined with its Vera Rubin GPU racks would deliver optimal performance across the entire spectrum of inference workloads. But, as we’ve discussed at length now, disaggregated compute architectures are not unique to Groq. Nvidia rival Cerebras is building similar systems with AWS and AMD, SambaNova is working with Intel, and d-Matrix and its partners are combining its in-memory compute platform with Nvidia GPUs to the same end as Nvidia’s Vera Rubin-LPX rack combo. The damage, if any, has been done Deals of this sort that are engineered to avoid regulatory scrutiny should get it anyway, several US senators have argued. While Nvidia didn’t outright buy Groq on paper, it may as well have. However, the real question for the DOJ is whether the deal was harmful to competition, and given the competitive landscape, proving harm may be easier said than done. But even if the DOJ found reason to litigate and was successful in unwinding the deal — it certainly wouldn’t be the first time regulators had torpedoed an Nvidia deal — it probably wouldn’t change much. Before Nvidia and Groq announced their licensing deal, the GPU giant was already laying the foundations for an ecosystem with its networking business at its center. In late 2024, the company contributed its MGX rack designs to the Open Compute Project (OCP) making it possible for any chipmaker to put their chips in racks originally designed for Nvidia GPUs. Then in mid-2025, GPUzilla opened its high-speed interconnect tech — the secret sauce that makes six dozen GPUs behave as one — to the broader industry through a licensing scheme called NVLink Fusion. As we recently discussed, the combination of open racks and Nvidia networking effectively meant that any chipmaker licensing the tech could slot their designs directly into Nvidia’s racks. If the DOJ blocked the acquihire and unwound the deal, Nvidia might lose direct control of LPU development and any revenues from the sale of the chips, but it wouldn’t necessarily be the end of its Groq LPX racks. Groq would just join the growing number of Nvidia hardware partners designing around the company’s AI factory ecosystem. In fact, if anything, the acquihire ensures that even if regulators eventually derail the deal, there will be plenty of alternatives lined up and ready to fill the void. ®
492b00c727b91f3c: HONG KONG, Sept 12 — China and Nepal have taken different approaches to information after a Himalayan flood, shaping what the public saw of a disaster that killed more than 1,400 people.
The August 26 tsunami-like surge of water, mud and debris from a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border left more than 5,650 missing, including hundreds of foreigners.
Both China and Nepal have gone after fabricated posts on the flood.
But Beijing has gone further to suppress eyewitness video footage and punish people challenging official figures, in an information crackdown that rights groups say follows a familiar pattern.

Information transmitted by Chinese state media on the flood gave little voice to the missing people’s relatives and focused on emergency workers’ recovery efforts in Tibet, where foreign journalists do not enjoy unfettered access.

Nepal has pressured social media platforms and news outlets to remove fabricated visuals — including some debunked by AFP fact-checkers — but Kathmandu offers regular updates of death tolls via social media. Direct commentary from families of victims is readily available on and offline.
Umesh Shrestha, chair of the independent regulatory body Press Council Nepal, said it had asked more than 100 social media accounts to remove content. Most obeyed.
“Things can spread very quickly,” Shrestha said.
Nepali police arrested one man who allegedly shared a fabricated donation to a relief fund to promote his personal account.
The disaster came just ahead of the one-year anniversary of anti-corruption protests that toppled the previous government, triggered by a social media ban.
China penalised 10 people accused of spreading falsehoods online, according to the Ministry of Public Security.
They include some who allegedly suggested the actual death toll was higher than official figures.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Offerings placed by workers to mourn the victims of the August 26 mudslide are seen at the site of the destroyed Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, in China’s western Tibet region on September 5, 2026. — CNS/China OUT/AFP pic
Beijing’s foreign ministry insists the release of information has been “open, transparent and timely”, and criticised what it has called “malicious smearing and sensationalism”.
It also organised a trip for a small number of foreign media to the Tibetan epicentre of the disaster.
‘Public panic’
AFP fact-checkers have debunked dozens of claims about the floods in multiple languages.
One video that falsely claimed to show the glacial and mountain collapse that caused the flooding – posted on Facebook and X – was filmed in Alaska’s Columbia Glacier days beforehand.
Other footage created using Google’s AI tools showed water breaching a riverbank and flooding streets and amassed tens of thousands of interactions.
“During disasters, public panic is high,” said Nepali investigative journalist Rabi Raj Baral, who is also a member of the Press Council Nepal.
But both Nepal and China have not only gone after fabrications, but have also targeted posts including some sharing genuine footage.
Nepali authorities have held talks with Meta and TikTok to speed up the removal of AI content, graphic images and fraudulent aid schemes.
Both platforms pay AFP to fact-check posts with potentially false information.
Video verified by AFP as showing the deluge engulfing Gyirong Port – the border post with Nepal – and other eyewitness content have largely disappeared from the Chinese internet.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Repair work has been paused along a road leading to Gyirong Port after a mudslide damaged it in Gyirong County, western Tibet, on August 28, 2026, amid the threat of new flooding. — AFP pic
Social media sites such as Douyin and Weibo have instead featured extensive state media coverage of search operations, without naming the missing or showing much footage of families’ reactions.
‘Atmosphere of mistrust’
AFP fact-checkers found flood-related misinformation is mostly absent from Chinese platforms, although conspiracy theories have blossomed abroad.

Posts shared from Canada to South Korea allege China lied about the death toll, and that its dam construction projects caused the disaster — even though scientists say a glacial collapse in Nepal was to blame.
Online critics also point to the fact that the vast bulk of the dead and missing reported by the two governments are in Nepal.

In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,369 bodies, while around 5,132 people are missing, according to the disaster agency Thursday. In China, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media.
The stark difference, however, may be a reflection of the disaster’s geography and scale.

The glacial mountain collapse occurred in downstream Nepal, sending a wave of debris so powerful it smashed China’s high-altitude border post in tightly restricted Tibet, before carving a path of destruction across Nepal.
Bodies on the Chinese side may have washed downstream too, but because of the geography, they could be buried in a thick layer of mud and debris that makes recovery impossible.
Aleksandra Bielakowska, a Taipei-based advocacy manager for Reporters Without Borders (RSF), said that Beijing’s restrictions had created an “atmosphere of mistrust”.
In contrast, Celia Mercier, head of RSF’s South Asia Desk, said Nepal had “largely treated misinformation as a problem within an otherwise relatively open information environment”. — AFP
ec6ddd48118d7177: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 12 — Rain and heavy traffic did little to dampen the warm atmosphere inside Barra Restaurant on Wednesday, where Spanish diplomats, chefs, and food lovers gathered to celebrate a shared appreciation for good food.
For Spain’s Ambassador-designate to Malaysia Sergi Farré Salvá, food offers a natural connection between Spain and Malaysia, a country where eating is deeply woven into everyday life.

“One of the first words that we learn when we come here in Bahasa Melayu is makan,” said Farré, who arrived in Malaysia a month ago. “So, we are going to do lots of makan-makan today,” he added, drawing laughter from the guests.
Farré called food a “universal connector” and described his first dining experience at Barra as more than simply a meal.
“It was a cultural experience, an artistic experience,” he said, highlighting the combination of tradition, creativity, and innovation that characterises Spanish gastronomy.
The ambassador-designate is expected to present his credentials to His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia, in late October or early November this year.
During the event, Farré officially presented the Restaurants From Spain certification plaque to Chef Gabriel Bonin, Chef Ignasi Prats, and the Barra team.

Awarded by the Spanish government through ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the certification recognises restaurants outside Spain that offer authentic, high-quality Spanish cuisine and promote Spanish culinary products and culture.
Farré said the certification was reserved for outstanding establishments and Barra’s inclusion had brought the number of certified Spanish restaurants in Kuala Lumpur to eight.
“That says a lot about Malaysia and what this capital stands for. Food happens 24 hours a day, seven days a week here. It is a paradise for any food lover,” he said.
